META.subject: Aviation
META.subtitle: Forces, lift, stalls, weight and balance, propellers and drag.

_note: Built before deck.py existed: cards are stored already expanded. Edit cards here; keep ids stable.

CARDS.front: In steady flight, the sum of all upward force components equals what?
CARDS.back: The sum of all downward force components
CARDS.extra: Not just lift versus weight. Every force has components, and all the up components balance all the down components.

CARDS.front: In steady flight, the sum of all forward force components equals what?
CARDS.back: The sum of all backward force components
CARDS.extra: Not just thrust versus drag.

CARDS.front: Which force does lift overcome?
Which part of the airplane creates lift?
Lift acts in which direction relative to the relative wind?
CARDS.extra: Relative wind is the airflow the wing meets; lift points at 90° to it.

CARDS.front: In straight-and-level flight at constant airspeed, lift equals which force?
CARDS.extra: Balanced flight.

CARDS.front: In straight-and-level flight at constant airspeed, thrust equals which force?
CARDS.extra: Balanced flight.

CARDS.front: When all forces are balanced, what happens to airspeed and altitude?
CARDS.extra: This is why balanced flight is straight, level and at constant airspeed.

CARDS.front: Balanced flight (no change in speed or altitude) illustrates which of Newton's laws?
CARDS.extra: An object keeps its motion unless an unbalanced force acts on it. The slide asks this as a discussion question.

CARDS.front: Which lift theory do the slides label false (NO!)?
Equal transit time theory claims air over the wing's top must do what?
CARDS.back: Travel faster to meet lower air at the trailing edge
CARDS.extra: The theory uses this to explain low pressure on top.

CARDS.front: What false assumption is equal transit time theory built on?
CARDS.back: Air splitting at the leading edge must rejoin together
CARDS.extra: Molecules arriving at the leading edge at the same time do NOT have to reach the trailing edge at the same time.

CARDS.front: On an airfoil, which edge is the front?
CARDS.extra: The back is the trailing edge.

CARDS.front: What is the symbol for angle of attack?
CARDS.extra: Also written AOA.

CARDS.front: How does a pilot change the angle of attack?
CARDS.back: By pitching the airplane up or down

CARDS.front: Why does a higher angle of attack create more lift?
An aircraft's airspeed is measured relative to what?
CARDS.back: The air it is moving through
CARDS.extra: Not relative to the ground.

CARDS.front: Why do higher airspeeds produce more lift?
CARDS.back: The airfoil contacts more air molecules

CARDS.front: Aircraft usually generate their own relative wind by creating which force?
CARDS.extra: Not always: a strong wind alone can create enough lift to make an aircraft fly.

CARDS.front: What does camber refer to on an airfoil?
How does a more curved camber line change lift?
What is the only way a pilot can change wing camber?
CARDS.extra: Flaps are lift-enhancing devices. Flaps down = more camber.

CARDS.front: How can pilots change the camber of the horizontal and vertical stabilizers?
CARDS.back: By moving the elevator and rudder
CARDS.extra: Deflecting a control surface curves the stabilizer's airfoil, changing its lift. The slide asks this as a discussion question.

CARDS.front: Doubling wing surface area does what to lift?
CARDS.extra: Area has a linear effect.

CARDS.front: Which lift factor can a pilot generally NOT control?
CARDS.extra: Pilots control AOA, airspeed and (with flaps) camber.

CARDS.front: Doubling an aircraft's velocity does what to lift?
CARDS.extra: Velocity's effect is exponential, not linear.

CARDS.front: A change in airspeed changes which value in the lift equation?
As angle of attack increases, what happens to the coefficient of lift?
CARDS.back: It increases, until the critical AOA

CARDS.front: What happens when a wing exceeds its critical angle of attack?
CARDS.extra: Airflow separates from the top of the wing and lift drops.

CARDS.front: For a given airplane and configuration, a stall always occurs at the same what?
CARDS.extra: Stalls can still happen at different airspeeds.

CARDS.front: What sets the stall angle of attack for a given configuration?
CARDS.extra: Configuration means things like flap setting.

CARDS.front: A normal stall occurs at what load factor?
CARDS.extra: The same force you feel sitting in your chair.

CARDS.front: An accelerated stall occurs at what load factor?
Compared to a normal stall, an accelerated stall happens at what airspeed?
With wing washout, which part of the wing should stall first?
CARDS.extra: The tip stalls last.

CARDS.front: Washout keeps which control surfaces effective after part of the wing stalls?
CARDS.extra: It also warns the pilot the whole wing is about to stall.

CARDS.front: With washout, how does wingtip AOA compare to wing root AOA?
CARDS.extra: The wing is twisted so the tip stalls last.

CARDS.front: What is another name for the center of lift?
What is the center of lift?
CARDS.back: The point where lift forces are concentrated

CARDS.front: For balance, where is the center of lift relative to the CG?
What is the datum?
CARDS.back: The point all arm measurements are taken from
CARDS.extra: Also called the reference datum.

CARDS.front: Who chooses the location of the datum?
CARDS.extra: It is an arbitrary point.

CARDS.front: In a balanced aircraft, positive plus negative moments at the CG equal what?
How do you find the moment of a weight?
CARDS.back: Multiply its arm by its weight
CARDS.extra: Arm is measured in inches from the datum.

CARDS.front: Find the CG: 100 at +50, 100 at +90, 200 at +150 (inches).
What is the danger of a CG too far forward?
CARDS.back: Not enough elevator nose-up force to flare for landing

CARDS.front: What is the danger of a CG too far aft?
CARDS.back: Not enough nose-down force for stall recovery
CARDS.extra: Especially at low airspeed.

CARDS.front: How does a pilot correct an out-of-limit CG?
A clockwise-spinning propeller causes what reaction from the airplane?
Torque reaction gives the airplane which turning tendency?
Torque reaction is an example of which of Newton's laws?
CARDS.extra: Engine torque is the action; the left gear forced downward is the reaction.

CARDS.front: When is torque reaction most prominent?
CARDS.back: Low speed with high power, like takeoff

CARDS.front: Why does torque effect lessen at higher airspeeds?
CARDS.back: Airflow over control surfaces counters it

CARDS.front: Why does a lower power setting reduce torque effect?
Why change a propeller's blade angle during flight?
CARDS.back: To keep the most efficient AOA at any speed
CARDS.extra: Blade angle is the propeller's pitch.

CARDS.front: What is the most common type of variable-pitch propeller?
For takeoff, the pilot sets which propeller pitch?
For cruise, the pilot sets which propeller pitch?
What does a variable-pitch propeller use to adjust its blades?
Where is the propeller control in the cockpit?
CARDS.back: A knob or lever next to the throttle

CARDS.front: What creates skin friction drag?
CARDS.back: Air resistance moving across the airplane's surface
CARDS.extra: The skin catches air particles and tries to pull the air along.

CARDS.front: Why does even a smooth surface create skin friction drag?
CARDS.back: It is rough at the microscopic level

CARDS.front: Parasite drag varies in proportion to what?
Parasite drag at 160 knots is how many times that at 80 knots?
CARDS.extra: Double the airspeed, square the effect: 2² = 4.

CARDS.front: What is the L/D ratio?
CARDS.back: Lift produced divided by drag created

CARDS.front: What does a higher L/D ratio mean?
CARDS.back: The aircraft produces lift more efficiently

CARDS.front: Ground effect occurs when the ground interferes with what?
Ground effect is most pronounced within what distance of the ground?
Ground effect is actually a reduction of which type of drag?
To a pilot, what does ground effect feel like?
A vector is a quantity with ? and magnitude.
CARDS.back: A vector is a quantity with direction and magnitude.
CARDS.extra: Vectors are drawn as arrows: the arrow points the direction, its length shows the magnitude.

CARDS.front: A vector is a quantity with direction and ?.
CARDS.back: A vector is a quantity with direction and magnitude.
CARDS.extra: Vectors are drawn as arrows: the arrow points the direction, its length shows the magnitude.

CARDS.front: Newton's third law: for every action there is an ?.
CARDS.back: Newton's third law: for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction.
CARDS.extra: Example: a rocket launch, or a propeller's torque reaction.

CARDS.front: The effect of velocity on lift is linear or exponential?, not linear.

CARDS.extra: Doubling velocity quadruples lift.

CARDS.front: An accelerated stall can happen in a ? or a quick pull-up.
